text: Every chapter in this course has deferred some version of the question: but does this actually work better than classical methods? This lesson answers it directly, using the fair-benchmark standard from Lesson 21 to separate what's proven from what's promising from what's marketing.

Applying that standard to the published literature: on small instances, QAOA has been shown to find good approximate solutions, consistent with this course's own simulated results. What has not been shown is QAOA outperforming the best classical heuristics at industrially relevant scale, when benchmarked fairly. Several published comparisons that initially looked favorable to QAOA were later found, on closer examination, to have compared against under-tuned classical baselines -- exactly Lesson 21's first failure mode in practice. VQE has reliably reproduced known energies for small molecules like H2 and LiH, but it hasn't outperformed coupled-cluster theory on anything of practical chemical interest.

Quantum advantage has a precise meaning: a demonstrated case where a quantum computer solves some problem faster than any known classical method, on real hardware, for a real task. This has been claimed for a small number of deliberately non-practical sampling problems, random circuit sampling being the most famous. No such claim has been made or defended for combinatorial optimization or quantum finance -- not because researchers haven't tried, but because the comparisons, when run fairly, haven't shown it yet.

For this picture to shift, several things plausibly need to happen together: substantially larger and less noisy hardware moving past today's noisy intermediate-scale devices, better optimizer techniques that avoid barren plateaus at scale, and identification of a specific problem structure where quantum methods have a provable or strongly empirical edge. None of this is guaranteed on any particular timeline, and honest reporting treats that uncertainty as a feature of the current state of knowledge, not something to paper over.

Next lesson's lab runs an actual fair benchmark yourself, end to end, across four methods -- brute force, greedy, simulated annealing, and simulated QAOA -- applying every one of Lesson 21's fairness checks to your own results.
